newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Stocks dragged down but dollar resilient.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Stocks dragged down but dollar resilient.

text.p: Europe's major equity markets and Wall Street all succumbed to selling pressure on Wednesday but the dollar weathered a big surge in Japan's trade surplus.
Both the London and Paris bourses were down more than one percent at one point, but they pulled well off their lows during the afternoon even though Wall Street made a weak start.
By the time Europe closed for the day, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was off around 45 points, or 0.58 percent, following profit-taking and earnings warnings from two technology companies.

The dollar briefly fell through 113 yen in European afternoon trade, revisiting levels seen earlier in Asia, but it recovered later and traders said it appeared resilient in the face of a big surge in Japan's trade surplus in May.
Japan's Finance Ministry said the surplus zoomed more than 220 percent in May from a year earlier and the balance with the United States rose 93 percent.
European traders said they were wary of adding to their short dollar positions before a meeting of the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrial nations that starts on Friday.
By 1600 GMT the dollar was quoted at 1.7330 marks and 113.48 yen, compared with 1.7335 and 113.37 in late European trade on Tuesday.

Equity markets saw London's blue-chip FTSE 100 index continue this week's steep falls, unable to shake off interest rate worries, the declining Dow and concerns about the new Labour government's first budget next month.

British retail sales figures for May gave the market an early shock, showing a monthly rise of 1.1 percent compared with forecasts of a 0.2 percent increase. Analysts said an interest rate rise was now likely next month.
Fears that the government will scrap an important tax break for pension funds has triggered a 125 point selloff in the blue chip FTSE 100 index since it posted a record close last Friday.
"It's been a recipe for gloom," one dealer said. "The interest rate situation certainly doesn't look supportive and the budget is casting a shadow over the market."
The FTSE managed to haul itself up from its day's lows in afternoon trade as the Dow pared its losses, but still closed 25.2 points lower at 4,657.0.
Paris fared little better, with traders citing investor caution ahead of new Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's parliamentary debut on Thursday.
The CAC-40 blue-chip index ended down 0.39 percent, or 10.86 points, at 2,751.74. The CAC-40 futures contract finished three points down at 2,748.
Analysts said it was unclear whether Jospin would elaborate significantly on economic policy and his privatisation plans after only two weeks in government and ahead of an audit of state finances.

Drink and luxury goods group LVMH came off its lows but ended 1.7 percent down at 1,507 francs after announcing on Tuesday it had bought 0.23 percent of GrandMet but did not plan to make an offer for the British drinks company.
Germany's 30-share DAX index also weakened, but less than its major European rivals, closing down 11.21 points, or 0.3 percent, at 3,730.27 during bourse floor trade.
The IBIS DAX recouped some ground in later screen trading and ended up 9.38 points at 3,730.56.
Traders said the market was unable to generate any upward impetus in the absence of new corporate data.
CURRENCIES AT 1600 GMT
The dollar was at 1.7330 marks and 113.48 yen, compared with 1.7335 and 113.37 in late European trade on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS -- CLOSING INDICES
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index closed down 25.2 points, or 0.54 percent, at 4,657.2.
PARIS - The CAC-40 closed down 10.86 points, or 0.39 percent, at 2,751.74.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed down 11.21 points, or 0.3 percent, at 3,730.27. The IBIS DAX ended later screen-based trade up 9.38 points at 3,730.56.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold closed at $341.55, down 80 cents. Silver ended at $4.73, down seven cents. Platinum closed down $9.50 at $410.0, while palladium finished down $3.50 at $194.
